slides.title: Calculator check — sine
slides.summary: Four quick problems in DEG mode. Enter each on your calculator before answers are revealed.

quizQuestions.prompt: Using a scientific calculator in Degrees (DEG), enter Sin(60). What number do you get?
quizQuestions.explanation: sin 60° ≈ 0.866 — used when checking sling leg tension at a 60° leg angle.

quizQuestions.prompt: Still in DEG mode, enter Sin(45). What number do you get?
quizQuestions.explanation: sin 45° ≈ 0.707 — matches the ≈7/10 safe-load example from the previous slide.

quizQuestions.prompt: In DEG mode, enter Sin(30). What number do you get?
quizQuestions.explanation: sin 30° = 0.500 — a 30° leg angle doubles tension per leg (T = W).

quizQuestions.prompt: What is 1 divided by 0.866?
quizQuestions.explanation: 1 ÷ sin 60° ≈ 1.155 — the tension multiplier per leg at a 60° angle.

slides.title: Length ÷ height — 45°
slides.summary: At a 45° leg angle, compare sling length (L) to vertical height (H).

sections.heading: 45° example
items: Vertical height H = 10 ft · sling leg length L ≈ 14.1 ft
Both legs at 45° from horizontal — symmetric bridle

sections.heading: Tension

items.label: Length ÷ height → L ÷ H
14.1 ÷ 10 = 1.41 tension factor per leg

items: Pull harder than half the load — multiply weight by ~1.41

sections.heading: Reduction

items.label: Height ÷ length → H ÷ L

items: Flatter angle — less of your WLL is available

slides.focusCallout: L ÷ H = tension · H ÷ L = reduction

slides.title: L ÷ H quiz — 60°, 45°, 30°
slides.summary: Length ÷ height gives tension. Height ÷ length gives reduction. Work each before revealing.

quizQuestions.prompt: H = 10 ft, L = 11.55 ft (60° leg angle). What is L ÷ H?
quizQuestions.explanation: 11.55 ÷ 10 = 1.155 — tension factor per leg at 60°.

quizQuestions.prompt: H = 10 ft, L = 14.1 ft (45° leg angle). What is L ÷ H?
quizQuestions.explanation: 14.1 ÷ 10 = 1.41 — tension factor per leg at 45°.

quizQuestions.prompt: H = 10 ft, L = 20 ft (30° leg angle). What is L ÷ H?
quizQuestions.explanation: 20 ÷ 10 = 2.000 — tension factor per leg at 30°.

quizQuestions.prompt: H = 10 ft, L = 14.1 ft (45° leg angle). What is H ÷ L?
quizQuestions.explanation: 10 ÷ 14.1 = 0.71 — reduction factor (~7/10 safe load) at 45°.

slides.title: Removal Criteria
slides.summary: Remove the hook from service immediately if any of the following are found:
slides.source: ASME B30.10 — Hooks (Current Edition)

sections.heading: Remove immediately
items: Cracks, fractures, or unauthorized weld repairs
Throat opening increased by more than 5% (max 6 mm / ¼ in. unless manufacturer specifies otherwise)
More than 10% wear of the original cross-section
Any visible bend or twist from the original plane of the hook
Excessive corrosion, pitting, or other damage affecting strength

items.label: Damaged, missing, or non-functioning safety latch (where required)
Missing or illegible manufacturer or WLL markings

items: Any condition identified by the manufacturer as requiring removal

slides.focusCallout: When in doubt, tag it out. Never attempt to straighten, heat, weld, or repair a hook unless specifically permitted by the manufacturer and applicable standards.

slides.title: Removal Criteria
slides.summary: Remove the chain sling from service immediately if any of the following are found:
slides.source: ASME B30.9 — Slings · ASME B30.26 — Rigging Hardware · manufacturer inspection criteria

sections.heading: Remove immediately
items: Cracked, broken, bent, twisted, or stretched links
Gouges, nicks, or excessive wear on any link
Wear exceeding 10% of the original link diameter
Elongation or deformation beyond the manufacturer's allowable limits
Evidence of heat damage — discoloration, weld spatter, arc strikes, or high-temperature exposure

items.label: Severe corrosion or pitting that reduces the chain's strength
Damaged or missing identification tag — grade, size, WLL, or serial number

items: Damaged hooks, master links, coupling links, or other sling components
Any condition identified by the manufacturer as requiring removal

slides.focusCallout: Never weld, heat, straighten, or repair alloy hoisting chain unless performed by the manufacturer or a qualified repair facility authorized by the manufacturer.

slides.title: Required Identification Tag
slides.summary: Under ASME B30.9 and common manufacturer requirements, a chain bridle sling must have a permanently affixed, durable identification tag.
slides.source: ASME B30.9 — Slings

items.label: Rated Working Load Limit (WLL) for the applicable hitch(es) and sling angle(s)
Tag is missing or illegible

slides.focusCallout: This is one of the few sling types where reach (length) and number of legs are specifically required as part of the sling identification because they directly affect the sling's rated capacity.

slides.title: Understanding Bridle Sling Capacity
slides.source: WorkSafeBC OHS Regulation 15.33; ASME B30.9 — Slings

sections.heading: Capacity
items: Bridle slings may have 2, 3, or 4 legs

items.label: The load is not always shared equally between all legs

items: Sling angle has a significant effect on leg tension and overall capacity

items.label: For WLL calculations, a 4-leg bridle sling is rated as a 3-leg sling

items: The WLL of the sling assembly is limited by the lowest-rated component
Every leg, fitting, and master link must have adequate capacity for the lift

slides.focusCallout: Never assume all four legs carry the load equally. Always calculate the lift using the applicable sling angle and the rated capacity of a three-leg bridle.

slides.title: Basic Load Calculations
slides.summary: Always calculate load share, tension multiplier, and actual leg tension — then verify the leg WLL exceeds the calculated tension.

sections.heading: 1. Load Share
items: Load per Leg = Total Load ÷ Number of Loaded Legs
Example: 6,000 lb ÷ 2 = 3,000 lb per leg (before sling angle is considered)

sections.heading: 2. Tension Multiplier (Derating)
items: Leg Tension = Load per Leg × Tension Multiplier
L = Sling Length · H = Vertical Height · θ = Sling Angle (from horizontal)

sections.heading: Remember
items: Verify the leg WLL exceeds the calculated tension

slides.focusCallout: As the sling angle decreases, leg tension increases. A smaller angle = greater derating and higher forces in each sling leg.

slides.title: Common Sling Angles
slides.summary: Leg Tension = (Load ÷ Number of Loaded Legs) × Tension Multiplier
slides.source: WorkSafeBC OHSR Table 15-3 · ASME B30.9 — Slings

items.label: BC Regulation — Uses derating based on angle from the vertical (Table 15-3)
Industry best practice (ASME B30.9) — Do not use sling angles below 30° from the horizontal unless approved by the manufacturer or a qualified person

slides.focusCallout: Lower angle = higher leg tension.

slides.title: Calculator check — tension
slides.summary: Four quick problems. Use the tension multiplier chart. Work each before answers are revealed.

quizQuestions.prompt: What is the tension multiplier for a 45° sling angle (from horizontal)?
quizQuestions.explanation: At 45° from horizontal, the tension multiplier is 1.41 (L ÷ H or 1 ÷ sin 45°).

quizQuestions.prompt: A 6,000 lb load is on a 2-leg bridle. What is the load share per leg before sling angle is considered?
quizQuestions.explanation: Load per leg = Total Load ÷ Number of Loaded Legs → 6,000 ÷ 2 = 3,000 lb.

quizQuestions.prompt: 6,000 lb load · 2-leg bridle · 45° sling angle. What is the tension in each sling leg?
8,000 lb load · 2-leg bridle · 30° sling angle. What is the tension in each sling leg?
quizQuestions.explanation: Leg tension = (8,000 ÷ 2) × 2.00 = 4,000 × 2.00 = 8,000 lb — each leg carries the full load weight at 30°.

slides.title: Common Hitch Configurations
slides.summary: *Typical rated capacity when the manufacturer's tag does not specify otherwise.
slides.source: ASME B30.9 — Slings · WSTDA WS-1 — Synthetic Web Slings · WSTDA RS-1 — Synthetic Roundslings

sections.heading: Configurations

items.label: Vertical Hitch · 100%
Basket Hitch · 200%

items: Basket Hitch (Inclined Legs) · Apply Sling Angle Derating

items.label: Double Wrap Hitch · Use Manufacturer's WLL

sections.heading: Key Points
items: Vertical Hitch – One sling leg supports the load
Basket Hitch – Up to 200% capacity when both legs are vertical and the load is balanced
Basket Hitch (Inclined Legs) – Capacity decreases as the sling angle decreases

items.label: Double-Leg Choker Hitch – Twice the single choker rating (150% web / roundsling)

sections.heading: Remember

items.label: Always use the manufacturer's sling tag to determine the Working Load Limit (WLL)

items: Consider both the hitch type and sling angle when calculating sling capacity
Protect synthetic slings from sharp edges

slides.title: Vertical vs Inclined Basket Legs
slides.summary: Vertical legs can use the full basket rating. Inclined legs require sling-angle derating.
slides.source: ASME B30.9 · WSTDA WS-1 / RS-1 · WorkSafeBC OHSR Part 15 · BC Crane Safety

sections.heading: 1. Vertical legs
items: Basket rating = up to 200% of the vertical hitch WLL
Both legs plumb and the load balanced

sections.heading: 2. Inclined legs
items: Do not use the full 200% basket rating
Effective capacity = Basket WLL ÷ (L ÷ H)  or  × sin(θ)

sections.heading: Best practices
items: Keep basket legs as vertical as practical
Use a spreader or longer reach when the angle would go shallow
Verify hitch type and angle against the sling tag WLL

slides.focusCallout: Inclined legs ≠ 200%. Apply sling-angle derating before you lift.

slides.title: Choke & basket math quiz
slides.summary: Use hitch ratings from the tag. Work each before revealing. Vertical WLL = 10,000 lb unless noted.

quizQuestions.prompt: Vertical WLL = 10,000 lb. Basket hitch with both legs vertical and the load balanced. What is the rated capacity?
quizQuestions.explanation: Vertical basket rating = 200% of vertical WLL → 10,000 × 2.00 = 20,000 lb.

quizQuestions.prompt: Vertical WLL = 10,000 lb. Single choker hitch on a synthetic web sling (choke angle ≥ 120°). What is the rated capacity?
quizQuestions.explanation: Web sling single choker ≈ 75% of vertical → 10,000 × 0.75 = 7,500 lb (unless the tag says otherwise).

quizQuestions.prompt: Vertical WLL = 10,000 lb. Single choker hitch on a polyester roundsling (choke angle ≥ 120°). What is the rated capacity?
quizQuestions.explanation: Polyester roundsling single choker ≈ 75% of vertical → 10,000 × 0.75 = 7,500 lb.

quizQuestions.prompt: One web sling in a double-leg (two-leg) choker hitch. Vertical WLL = 10,000 lb. What is the rated capacity?
quizQuestions.explanation: One-sling / double-leg choker = 2 × single choker. Web or roundsling: 2 × 75% = 150% → 10,000 × 1.50 = 15,000 lb.

slides.title: Double Wrap & Double Choke
slides.summary: Loads made of 2 or more pieces over 3 m (10 ft) long must be double wrapped and choked — OHSR 15.40.
slides.source: WorkSafeBC OHSR 15.40 — Slinging loads

items.label: 2 or more pieces of material
Each piece over 3 m (10 ft) long

sections.heading: Required method

items.label: Use a 2-legged sling arrangement

items: Position the slings to keep the load horizontal during the lift

items.label: Each sling must be choked around the load with a double wrap

sections.heading: Remember

items.label: Double wrap + choke = grip that resists slip and bundle shift

items: Select and use the sling to prevent slipping or overstressing (OHSR 15.40(1))
Protect synthetic slings from sharp edges

slides.focusCallout: 2+ pieces · over 3 m (10 ft) · double wrap · choke each sling

slides.title: Never Hammer a Choke
slides.summary: Never force the choke eye down the sling. Hammering creates an acute choke angle, damages the sling, and drops capacity below the tagged choker rating.
slides.source: ASME B30.9 · WSTDA WS-1 / RS-1 / RS-2 · manufacturer instructions · WorkSafeBC OHSR Part 15

items.label: 120°–180° · × 1.00 (full choker rating)

sections.heading: Why never hammer

items.label: Forces an acute choke angle well below 120°

items: Damages sling body fibres at the choke point
Creates an unrated condition — capacity may be lower than any table predicts
Let the choke settle naturally as the load is lifted

sections.heading: Standards & practice

items.label: ASME B30.9 — choke angles under 120° need manufacturer or qualified-person ratings

items: WSTDA WS-1 / RS-1 / RS-2 — multiply choker WLL by the angle reduction factor
Manufacturer instructions — do not hammer, pound, or force a choke
OHSR Part 15 — select and use slings to prevent slipping or overstressing

slides.focusCallout: Let the choke set naturally — never hammer it down.

slides.title: Opposing Chokes
slides.summary: Two choker hitches placed in opposite directions improve load stability and help prevent rolling or slipping on cylindrical loads.
slides.source: ASME B30.9 – Slings; WSTDA WS-1 – Synthetic Web Slings; WSTDA RS-1 – Synthetic Roundslings

sections.heading: When to Use Opposing Chokes

items.label: Two choker hitches are placed in opposite directions around the load

items: Used to improve load stability and help prevent the load from rolling or slipping
Commonly used on pipe, poles, logs, structural steel, and other cylindrical loads
Position the chokes so they are evenly spaced and the load remains balanced
Ensure both sling legs share the load as equally as possible

sections.heading: Remember
items: Use adequate edge protection where required
The WLL is limited by the lowest-rated component and the manufacturer's hitch rating

items.label: Opposing chokes improve stability, not the sling's rated capacity

slides.focusCallout: Opposing chokes improve stability — not the sling's rated capacity.

slides.title: Personnel Manbaskets & DEPs
slides.summary: Personnel platforms must be PE-designed and certified, permanently marked, and supported by rigging with a minimum 10:1 design factor.
slides.source: WorkSafeBC OHSR Part 14 / Part 15 · ASME B30.23 — Personnel Lifting Systems · manufacturer instructions

sections.heading: Design Requirements

items.label: Designed and certified by a Professional Engineer
All supporting rigging — minimum Design Factor 10:1 (Breaking Strength ÷ WLL)

items: Bridle legs connected to a master link or shackle so the load is shared between the legs
Inspect the platform and all rigging before every lift

sections.heading: Platform must be permanently marked with

items.label: Working Load Limit (WLL)

slides.focusCallout: Personnel lifting requires a 10:1 design factor for all supporting rigging.

slides.title: Personnel Manbaskets & DEPs
slides.summary: When hoisting personnel, keep the crane at or below 50% of rated capacity and include every suspended component in the all-up weight.
slides.source: WorkSafeBC OHSR Part 14 / Part 15 · ASME B30.23 — Personnel Lifting Systems · manufacturer instructions

sections.heading: Crane Capacity & All-Up Weight

items.label: Do not load the crane beyond 50% of its rated capacity when lifting a personnel platform

items: Calculate crane capacity using the total suspended load — not just the occupants
Lift personnel smoothly with continuous communication

sections.heading: All-Up Weight includes
items: Slings, shackles, master links, and all rigging

items.label: 10:1 Design Factor — applies to platform rigging (slings, shackles, master links). Minimum breaking strength must be at least 10 × all-up weight
50% Crane Capacity — separate WorkSafeBC limit on how much of the crane's rated capacity may be used when hoisting personnel

slides.focusCallout: 10:1 Design Factor ≠ 50% Crane Capacity

slides.title: Design Factor vs Breaking Strength vs WLL
slides.source: ASME B30.9 — Slings; WorkSafeBC OHSR Part 15

items.label: Breaking Strength — load at which the sling or component is expected to fail
Design Factor — Breaking Strength ÷ WLL
WLL — maximum load permitted during normal service

sections.heading: Example
items: Grade 80 alloy chain: 20,000 lb ÷ 4 = 5,000 lb WLL

items.label: Always use the manufacturer's tag — never estimate breaking strength
Personnel platforms require 10:1 supporting rigging under WorkSafeBC (not 4:1 / 5:1)

slides.focusCallout: Never calculate WLL from an estimated breaking strength — use the manufacturer's tag.

slides.title: Calculator check — strength & WLL
slides.summary: Four quick problems. Use WLL = Breaking Strength ÷ Design Factor. Work each before answers are revealed.

quizQuestions.prompt: A wire rope sling has a Minimum Breaking Strength of 25,000 lb. Design factor = 5. What is the WLL?
quizQuestions.explanation: WLL = Breaking Strength ÷ Design Factor → 25,000 ÷ 5 = 5,000 lb.

quizQuestions.prompt: A Grade 80 alloy chain sling has a Minimum Breaking Strength of 20,000 lb. Design factor = 4. What is the WLL?
quizQuestions.explanation: WLL = Breaking Strength ÷ Design Factor → 20,000 ÷ 4 = 5,000 lb.

quizQuestions.prompt: A wire rope sling is tagged for 8,000 lb WLL. Design factor = 5. What Minimum Breaking Strength is required?
quizQuestions.explanation: Breaking Strength = WLL × Design Factor → 8,000 × 5 = 40,000 lb.

quizQuestions.prompt: An alloy chain sling is tagged for 6,000 lb WLL. Design factor = 4. What Minimum Breaking Strength is required?
quizQuestions.explanation: Breaking Strength = WLL × Design Factor → 6,000 × 4 = 24,000 lb.

slides.title: Calculator check — material weights
slides.summary: Four new problems — not the lesson examples. Use the density / LF / sheet chart. Work each before answers are revealed.

quizQuestions.prompt: A pile of wet sand is about 8 ft × 4 ft × 2 ft. Wet sand ≈ 120 lb/ft³. About what is the weight?
quizQuestions.explanation: Volume = 8 × 4 × 2 = 64 ft³. Weight = 64 × 120 = 7,680 lb.

quizQuestions.prompt: You have 40 pieces of 2×4 lumber, each 16 ft long. Chart rate = 1.5 lb/LF. What is the total weight?
quizQuestions.explanation: Wt = lb/LF × length × count → 1.5 × 16 × 40 = 960 lb.

quizQuestions.prompt: A pallet has 15 sheets of 1/2 in 4×8 drywall. Chart says ≈ 54 lb per sheet. About what does the pallet weigh?
quizQuestions.explanation: 15 × 54 = 810 lb (banding/pallet weight not included).

quizQuestions.prompt: A steel plate is 6 ft × 3 ft × 1 in thick. Steel = 490 lb/ft³. What is the weight?
quizQuestions.explanation: Thickness = 1/12 ft. Volume = 6 × 3 × (1/12) = 1.5 ft³. Weight = 1.5 × 490 = 735 lb.

slides.title: Center of Gravity Symbol
slides.summary: The international CG mark — the balance point of the load.
slides.source: WorkSafeBC OHSR Part 14 · BC Crane Safety — rigger competency (OHSR Part 15)

sections.heading: International symbol
items: Circle divided into four quadrants — alternating red / white
Marks the load’s center of gravity (CG)

sections.heading: What CG means
items: The point where weight is evenly distributed on all sides
The balance point of the load in every direction
Loads rotate until CG hangs under the hook

sections.heading: Why it matters

items.label: Miss the CG → tilt, swing, unequal sling forces, shock loading

items: BC Crane Safety: riggers must assess load weight, stability, and balance before the lift (OHSR Part 15)

slides.focusCallout: Weight is evenly distributed on all sides of this point

slides.title: Offset Load — Sea Can CG
slides.summary: Answer: 12 ft toward the heavy side
slides.source: WorkSafeBC OHSR Part 14 · BC Crane Safety — rigger competency (OHSR Part 15)

sections.heading: Known
items: Crate offset → heavy side 3,000 lb · light side 1,000 lb

sections.heading: Answer
items: CG is 12 ft toward the heavy side

slides.focusCallout: Rule: Distance = (Heavy side ÷ Total) × Length

slides.title: Hook Directly Over CG
slides.summary: Always place the hook directly above the center of gravity.
slides.source: WorkSafeBC OHSR 14.46 — Vertical load line · BC Crane Safety — rigger competency

sections.heading: The rule

items.label: Hook ALWAYS directly over the center of gravity

items: Pick points / sling arrangement must keep CG under the hook
Test-lift a short distance to confirm balance before the full hoist

sections.heading: WorkSafeBC OHSR 14.46
items: Load line above the hook / load block must stay vertical
Prevents side-loading the crane and uncontrolled swing

sections.heading: If the hook is off the CG

items.label: Load tilts or swings until CG hangs under the hook

items: Unequal leg loading · shock · possible tip or drop
Changing CG during a lift is treated as a critical-lift condition under Part 14

slides.focusCallout: Hook must hang DIRECTLY over the center of gravity

quizQuestions.prompt: A 2-leg bridle is at 50°. The chart only shows 60°, 45°, and 30°. Which column do you use?
quizQuestions.explanation: Angle between chart values → always use the next LOWER column (50° → 45°).

quizQuestions.prompt: 2-leg bridle @ 45° chart capacity = 13,574 lb. The bridle is choked. What capacity do you use?
quizQuestions.explanation: Choked 2-leg bridle → multiply by 0.75 → 13,574 × 0.75 ≈ 10,180 lb.

quizQuestions.prompt: Wire rope Vertical = 4,700 lb. 2-leg @ 60°. Capacity ≈ Vertical × 2 × Sin(60°). About how much?
Two bridle legs are each 20 ft at 60° from horizontal. Equal leg lengths. Distance between attachments?
quizQuestions.explanation: Equal legs → equal angles. 60°+60° → top angle 60°. Equilateral triangle → distance = 20 ft.

slides.title: Taglines
slides.summary: Control the load from a safe distance — clean rope, gloves on, knots you trust.
slides.source: WorkSafeBC OHSR 14.28(5)

slides.title: Safe Tagline Practice
slides.summary: Keep the rope clean and yourself clear of the load path.
slides.source: WorkSafeBC OHSR 14.28(5) · OHSR 8.2 / 8.19 — hand protection

sections.heading: Gear & PPE
items: Keep the tagline clean — no mud, grease, or frays that cut grip

items.label: Wear gloves — OHSR 8.2 general-purpose work gloves; 8.19 if abrasion risk

items: Allow extra length — never run out mid-swing

sections.heading: Stance & slope
items: Stand about 1:1 from the load — distance ≈ height for a ~45° tagline slope
Aim for a clean ~45° slope — not straight out, not under the load
Hands on the load only at waist height — otherwise control with the rope

sections.heading: Regulation

items.label: OHSR 14.28(5) — use tag lines or other effective means when needed

items: Not every lift needs one — use them when movement or placement is hazardous without them

slides.focusCallout: OHSR 14.28(5) — tag lines when needed to control or position the load

slides.title: Allow Extra — Fixed Eye
slides.summary: Leave spare rope, and finish the working end with a knot that will not slip.

sections.heading: Why extra
items: Load swings, turns, and rises — you need spare line in hand
Never wrap the tagline around your wrist or body
Keep enough free length to step clear without letting go

sections.heading: Figure-eight on a bight
items: Double the rope to make a bight
Form a figure-eight and pull the bight through
Dress and snug — gives a strong fixed eye for hardware or a handhold

slides.focusCallout: Extra rope + a fixed eye beats a short line and a slipping hitch

slides.title: Knots for Taglines
slides.summary: Two hitches you will use constantly — clove for the load, bowline for a fixed loop.

sections.heading: Clove hitch
items: Fast attachment around pipe, rail, or load corner
Holds under steady pull — check it after every move

sections.heading: Bowline
items: Fixed loop that will not slip under load
Easy to untie after it has been loaded

sections.heading: Before you trust it
items: Dress the knot — no crossed strands left loose
Leave a working-end tail long enough to see
If it looks wrong, retie — do not fly a mystery knot

slides.focusCallout: Pick the knot for the job — then dress it before the lift

slides.title: Clove Hitch
slides.summary: Two wraps that cross — the working end tucks under the last turn.

sections.heading: How to tie
items: Pass the rope behind (or around) the bar / attachment
Bring it over the top and around again so the second wrap crosses the first
Tuck the working end under the second wrap (follow the arrow)
Pull both ends to dress — you should see a clear X on the face of the hitch

sections.heading: On the job
items: Standing part and working end exit opposite ways through the X
Re-check after the load shifts — cloves can walk if left loose
Add a half-hitch backup if the line will see shock or slack cycles

slides.focusCallout: Wrap · cross · tuck — then snug the X flat on the bar

slides.title: Bowline
slides.summary: Rabbit up the hole, around the tree, back down the hole — fixed eye that unties after loading.

sections.heading: How to tie
items: Make a small loop in the standing part (the rabbit hole)
Pass the working end up through the loop
Wrap it behind the standing part (around the tree)
Bring it back down through the loop and pull to dress

sections.heading: On the job
items: Leaves a fixed eye that will not slip like a slipknot
Still unties after it has taken load — good for tagline ends
Leave a visible tail; unfinished bowlines can capsize

slides.focusCallout: Up · around · back down — then dress the loop

slides.title: Critical Lift
slides.summary: Written plan on site. Brief the crew. Then hoist.
slides.source: WorkSafeBC OHSR 14.42.1 · critical lift definition · BC Crane Safety

sections.heading: It is critical when
items: Over 90% of capacity at more than half the max radius
Tandem lift — any crane over 75%, or more than two cranes
Lifting a person in a suspended platform
Load CG or sling length changes during the lift
Floating base, over live high voltage, or a submerged load

items: Write the plan — rigging, wind, speeds, load share, signallers
Hold a pre-job meeting and document who was briefed
Repeat the meeting if people or equipment change
Keep clear radio / signals for the whole lift
Keep the written plan available at the worksite
